body:
高市首相は１３日の衆院予算委員会で、自身を衆院選で支援しなかった地元首長の自治体の道路予算を「カットした」などと発言した簗農相について「行政の運営をしていいのかも含め、しっかりと考えさせていただく」と述べ、進退の判断に含みを持たせた。政府・自民党内で「辞任は避けられない」との見方が強まっており、首相は国会審議への影響も踏まえ、近く対応を判断する見通しだ。【表】一目でわかる…高市首相が簗農相の続投を判断した理由
予算委で首相は、簗氏の陣営が衆院選中に支持者をシャトルバスで無料送迎した問題では、簗氏から事情を聞き取るとし、「仮に違法性があれば、躊躇（ちゅうちょ）しない」と更迭を辞さない考えも示した。自民幹部は「国会審議への影響を避けるには、辞めてもらうしかない」と語った。
この日は首相と全閣僚が出席して基本的質疑が行われた。簗氏は、道路予算に関し「（国土交通省に）減額を求めた事実はない」と改めて釈明した。無料送迎問題では、野党から「公職選挙法違反ではないか」と追及を受けた。簗氏は、２０２４年と今年の衆院選で出陣式の出席者を臨時駐車場から会場までバスで送迎したことは認めつつ、「会場費の一部で、利益供与や寄付にはあたらない」と違法性を否定した。
簗氏は午前の予算委では、事前に陣営スタッフが地元の選挙管理委員会に問い合わせ、違法性がないことを確認したと答弁した。これに対し、栃木県選管は１３日午後、「問い合わせの有無については確認できない」とのコメントを発表した。読売新聞の取材に対し、こうした問い合わせがあった場合には「過去の実例や判例に基づき『公選法上の利益供与にあたるおそれがあるため、差し控えてほしい』と伝える」と説明した。
首相は１３日夜、簗氏から電話で無料送迎問題について報告を受けた。首相は予算委後、首相官邸で記者団に対し「まず電話で報告を受け、あす（１４日）の予算委後にも会えれば、話を聞きたい」と語っていた。
１４日には衆院予算委が開かれ、１６日と１９日には参院予算委が予定されている。自民内では、参院予算委前の進退判断を求める声が広がっている。

title: 大阪にアンソロ社データ拠点 調整
body: NTTが、米AI（人工知能）開発企業アンソロピック向けのデータセンターを大阪府内に建設する方向で協議していることが関係者への取材でわかった。建設費は1兆円規模とみられ、実現すれば国内最大級。アンソロピックにとってはアジア初のデータセンター拠点になりそうだ。【写真】アンソロピックのダリオ・アモデイ最高経営責任者（CEO）関係者によると、NTTデータグループが大阪府の沿岸部に受電容量500メガワットのデータセンターを建設する方向で調整を進めている。アンソロピックは昨秋、アジア太平洋地域で初めて東京にオフィスを開設。アジア地域で複数のデータセンター建設を目指しており、日本やアジアでの事業をさらに拡大する狙いがあるとみられる。

title: 横浜市で住宅火災 2遺体見つかる
body: 13日午後10時半ごろ、横浜市港北区大豆戸町の菱沼紀元さん（84）方から出火し、木造平屋建てが全焼した。隣接する住宅の一部も焼け、火は約5時間半後の14日午前4時ごろに消しとめられたが、横浜市消防局によると、火元から年齢や性別不明の2人の遺体が見つかった。現場はJR新横浜駅から北東に約800メートルの住宅街。（斎藤茂洋）

title: 停止義務ないのに違反に ミス63件
body: 東京都小平市の交差点で、本来は停止する義務がないのに、信号を無視したとする道路交通法違反容疑で警視庁が車両の運転者を誤って取り締まっていたことがわかった。取り締まりミスは2024年5月～26年7月に63件あり、都公安委員会は違反点数を是正した。警視庁は該当する運転者に納められた反則金を返還する。【画像】警察も間違えた交差点　「車は恐る恐る再発進」　現場は?取り締まりミスがあったのは、西武鉄道多摩湖線一橋学園駅北口付近の道路「学園中央通り」（東京都小平市学園東町1丁目）だ。東から西方面に線路に向かっていくと「A交差点」があり、A交差点の横断歩道手前に「停止線」が引かれている。A交差点の先には踏切がある。この踏切の手前には信号機と「踏切停止線」がある。踏切を越えた先には「B交差点」があり、この信号機は、踏切を含めB交差点の交通を規制するものだ。信号機は「赤点滅」「黄」「赤」の順で変わる。信号が赤点滅や赤の時、車両は「踏切停止線」の手前で一時停止や停止をする必要がある。しかし、管轄する小平署は、信号機が赤点滅や赤の時、A交差点の停止線で止まらなかった車両について、信号無視をしたとして取り締まったという。運転者は反則切符を切られ、都公安委員会から違反点数を付され、反則金を納めた。

title: AIに任せた仕事でミス 責任は誰に
body: （ブルームバーグ）:企業は生産性や効率の向上を目指し、AIシステムに任せる仕事の範囲を広げている。一方、AIが担う役割が増すにつれ、問題が起きた際に誰が責任を負うべきかは、経営幹部や管理職、従業員の間で明確になっていない。【写真を見る】AIに任せた仕事でミス、責任は誰に-企業で活用拡大も対応追いつかず米ペンシルベニア大学ウォートン校が13日に公表した新たな報告書によると、AIが重大なミスをした際の責任の所在について、管理職の見方は大きく分かれている。AIを使った従業員、その上司、会社のリスク管理部門に責任があるとの回答はいずれも約25％で、ほぼ拮抗した。ベンダーに責任があるとの回答は約10％で、誰が責任を負うべきか分からないとの回答も同程度だった。OpenAIやアルファベット傘下のグーグル、メタ・プラットフォームズなどが、性能を高めたAIエージェントを従業員向けに相次いで導入する中、誰が責任を負うのかが一段と重要な問題になっている。こうしたAIエージェントには企業内で独自のIDが与えられ、自ら目標に向けて作業を進めることができる。場合によっては数日間にわたり、自律的に作業することもある。ここ数カ月は、AIエージェントが制御不能に陥るリスクが注目されてきた。ただ、企業にとって差し迫ったリスクは、より身近なところにあるのかもしれない。従業員監視ソフトウエア会社テラマインドのバイスプレジデント、リーロン・ウォルター氏によると、AIエージェントが電子メールアカウントや顧客データベースなどにアクセスできる場合、プロンプトのわずかなミスや曖昧な指示が、たちまち大きな問題に発展する恐れがある。実際、企業ではこうしたミスがすでに起きているという。同氏によれば、全米で事業を展開するある小売企業で、従業員が顧客向けメールを自動送信するAIシステムを構築したところ、プロンプトのミスにより、6時間足らずで1万8000人を超える顧客に誤った返金やキャンセルの通知が送られた。その結果、顧客から数千件の問い合わせが寄せられた。

title: 道新記者をサハリンで拘束 露当局
body:
【モスクワ共同】ロシア連邦保安局（FSB）は13日、極東サハリン州で北海道新聞ユジノサハリンスク支局の男性記者をスパイ容疑で拘束したと発表した。ロシアの防衛能力に関する情報を収集したと主張し、記者を首都モスクワに移送し逮捕。モスクワの裁判所は2カ月の勾留を認めた。タス通信などが報じた。【写真】「ロシア兵器9割に日本部品」　ミサイルや無人機に転用　名指しされた日本企業13社
スパイ罪は法定刑が懲役10～20年の重罪。FSBが主張する「スパイ容疑」は取材の範囲内だった可能性があるが、ロシア当局が国外追放といった措置でなく、勾留を決めたことから、拘束が長期化する懸念がある。FSBは記者の拘束時や支局を捜索する際の映像も公開した。ロシア外務省によると、記者は13日に拘束された。FSBは、記者が日本の情報機関の指示でクリール諸島（千島列島と北方領土）からウクライナへの「特別軍事作戦」に動員された兵士や志願兵の人数に関する情報を収集し、伝達しようとしていたと指摘した。北海道新聞は現在、日本メディアで唯一、日本人記者をサハリンに常駐させている。

title: ローマ教皇手術 肺腺がんを確認
body: 【ローマ共同】ローマ教皇庁（バチカン）は13日、イタリア・ローマの病院で同日行われた教皇レオ14世（71）の肺結節の手術が成功したと発表した。執刀医らの報告として、教皇は右肺下部を切除し、組織検査で肺腺がんが確認されたと明らかにした。教皇庁は予定通りの時間、方法で完了したとしている。手術前には、約1週間は入院を続ける見込みとしていた。教皇は11日、検査で肺の結節が非常に早期の段階で見つかり、手術を受けると明らかにした。レオ14世は昨年5月、米国出身者として初めて教皇に選出された。テニス好きとして知られ、これまで健康問題は指摘されてこなかった。

title: 韓国で切り付け事件 1人心肺停止
body: 韓国のソウル近郊・仁川の商業施設で13日午後、切りつけ事件があり、8人がケガをし、このうち1人が心肺停止だということです。【画像】切りつけ事件があった現場　男は刃物を両手に縛り付けた状態で犯行との情報も韓国の聯合ニュースによりますと、午後1時40分ごろ、韓国・仁川にある大型の商業施設で、男が施設の中にいた人々を刃物で切りつけました。これにより8人がケガをし、病院で手当てを受けていますが、このうち1人が心肺停止の状態だということです。警察は、60代とみられる男の身柄を拘束し、詳しい当時の状況を調べているということです。仁川には、日本人観光客も多く利用する仁川空港がありますが、今回現場となった商業施設までは20キロ以上離れています。在韓国日本大使館と韓国警察によりますと、日本人の負傷者はいないということです。

title: 写真大手ゲッティ 米破産法申請へ
body:
【ニューヨーク共同】米写真・映像販売大手ゲッティイメージズ・ホールディングスは13日までに、米連邦破産法11条（日本の民事再生法に相当）の適用を申請すると発表した。スポーツを含めた主要国際ニュースの報道写真に強みを持つものの、多額の負債が経営を圧迫した。人工知能（AI）による生成画像との競争激化が懸念される中、投資会社の支援を得て非上場化し、経営再建を目指す。【写真】中国企業に買われた「東芝ブランド」その後　19年
破産法適用の申請は数週間以内に行う。申請後も、事業は通常通り継続する。写真家など画像提供者や顧客、従業員への影響についても想定していないと説明している。ゲッティは報道写真や動画サービスの分野で、ロイター通信やAP通信などと競合関係にある。

title: ウ軍 なぜ露のデータセンター攻撃
body:
ウクライナ軍は今年、ドローン部隊の増強によって、ロシア社会に大混乱をもたらしました。
製油所の集中砲火から次には、ネット通販の物流拠点、そして10月に入って、「ロシア版Google」と言われるネット大手「Yandex」のデータセンターの３つを破壊しました。
4月のホルムズ海峡危機で、イランはドローン攻撃によりUAEのアマゾンデータセンターを破壊しましたが、9月、保管データの復旧が不可能になったと発表されました。
現代のドローン戦争は防御が甘いITインフラが標的となり、ネット社会が麻痺するリスクを露呈しています。
戦争ではデータセンターが標的に　ロシア軍がキーウの施設を相次いで攻撃　デジタルインフラの防御策は？ #エキスパートトピ出典：佐々木正明　2026/9/30(水)
イランによるAmazonのデータセンターへの攻撃により顧客データが永久に失われる出典：GIGAZINE　2026/9/17(木)
Ukraine’s Strikes on Yandex Data Centers, Explained出典：The Moscow Times　2026/10/12(月)
Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський@ZelenskyyUa
Yandexの主要データセンターは露国内に６つ。うち3カ所が破壊されました。
地図やネット決済、クラウドサービスなどに支障をもたらし、完全復旧まで数か月かかると予測されています。しかし、その間にも残りの施設が攻撃される可能性があります。
①大規模データセンターはどこにあるか広く知られており、防御が手薄。ネット社会への混乱が長引けば露経済全体に大きな損失をもたらす。国民の厭戦機運が高まり、批判の矢は戦争継続最優先のプーチン政権へと向かう。②ゼレンスキー大統領は自動化された露からのメッセージ通信量が急落したと主張。「250分の１」という。露のハイブリット攻撃への防御手段となりうる。③Yandexサービスは近隣諸国のカザフスタンなどにも普及し、余波が広がっている。親露国からも停戦要求圧力が高まる可能性がある。④ウ軍の攻撃の理由は、露軍が先月、ウ国内のデータセンターを破壊したことへの報復。「目には目を」の再報復への抑止力になる。⑤すでに露国内では欧州地域にあるデータセンターを東方のシベリア奥地へと分散移動させる「セットバック」論がでており、この移設にも相当の費用がかかる。

title: 九州新幹線 全線で運転再開
body: 電力設備の損傷で13日、終日運転を見合わせていた九州新幹線の鹿児島中央と熊本の間は、14日の始発から通常通り運転を再開しました。【写真を見る】再開を待っていた人たち…鹿児島中央駅、けさの様子福岡〜熊本間は13日運転を再開していて、九州新幹線は全線で通常運転となりました。■【運転見合わせ　経緯は】熊本市の熊本総合車両所で12日午後10時ごろ、九州新幹線の点検中に、「すり板」と呼ばれる部品がなくなっているのが確認されました。ほかの車両に問題がないか確認し、およそ5時間後の13日午前3時ごろから一部の車両は徐行運転で運転を再開していました。その後、パンタグラフや架線を含む電力設備の点検を行うため、九州新幹線は13日始発から運転を見合わせ、当初は13日夕方からの全線で運転再開見込みと発表していました。福岡〜熊本間については13日午後4時16分に運転が再開されましたが、熊本駅近くでは、電力設備の損傷も見つかり、熊本〜鹿児島中央間は、13日は終日運転見合わせとなっていました。

title: 日本のGDP 来年世界6位の見込み
body:
【ワシントン＝坂本幸信、バンコク＝田畑清二】日本の名目国内総生産（ＧＤＰ）が、２０２７年にインドと英国の両方に抜かれて世界６位となる見込みとなった。国際通貨基金（ＩＭＦ）が１２日に公表した最新の世界経済見通しで明らかになった。４月の前回見通し時点では、英国が日本を抜く時期は２９年としていたが、前倒しとなりそうだ。【地図】インドの乗用車販売、「代替燃料車」がガソリン車を逆転
ＩＭＦの推計によると、日本の名目ＧＤＰは２６年時点で４兆３４１９億ドル、２７年時点で４兆４６７６億ドルとなる。インドは２６年時点では４兆６０２億ドルと日本と英国に続く６位だが、２７年には４兆５２１１億ドルとなり、米国、中国、ドイツに次ぐ４位となる見通しだ。英国も２６年時点の４兆２６８４億ドルから２７年時点で４兆４８８９億ドルとなり、日本を抜く予想となった。
インド、英国ともに日本よりも高い経済成長が見込まれていることに加え、日本にとっては対ドルの円相場で円安・ドル高傾向が続いていることも響くとみられている。
ＩＭＦは２６年の世界全体の経済成長率については３・１％と予想し、７月時点の予想から０・１ポイント上方修正した。人工知能（ＡＩ）関連の需要拡大がエネルギー価格の高騰による悪影響を相殺していると分析している。日本は２６年が０・１ポイント上方修正され、０・７％となった。

title: 都営地下鉄談合 5社に排除命令へ
body: 都営地下鉄などの軌道保守工事を巡る入札で談合を繰り返したとして、公正取引委員会は13日、工事を受注した6社の独占禁止法違反（不当な取引制限）を認定し、うち5社に再発防止を求める排除措置命令を出す方針を固めた。各社には、計約5億円の課徴金納付も命じる方針。関係者への取材で判明した。【図で見る】都営地下鉄の保守工事で談合疑い（25年11月）排除措置命令を受けるのは、JR東日本の関係会社の東鉄工業（東京都品川区）▽坪井工業（同中央区）▽早川建設（同台東区）▽日信工業（川崎市）▽JR九州建設グループの三軌建設（福岡市）。東急電鉄グループの東急軌道工業（川崎市）は課徴金減免制度（リーニエンシー）が適用され、排除措置命令と課徴金納付命令を免れる見込み。公取委は既に処分案を通知し、意見を聴取した上で最終決定する。公取委は発注側の東京都交通局についても、談合への関与の有無を調べているとみられる。入札情報の漏えいなどが確認されれば、公取委が都に対し、官製談合防止法に基づく改善措置を求める可能性もある。6社は遅くとも2020年3月以降、都営線の大江戸線と浅草線、三田線、新宿線の地下鉄4路線のほか、東京さくらトラム（都電荒川線）、新交通システムの日暮里・舎人ライナーの軌道保守工事を巡る希望制指名競争入札などで、担当者間で入札前に受注予定社を調整し、互いの競争を制限したとされる。各路線を所管する都交通局は、老朽化したレールや線路を切り替える分岐器の交換といったメンテナンスなどを民間に委託している。入札は、都交通局が技術的な条件などを提示して公募し、審査で選ばれた事業者が参加できる。入札は路線ごとに実施され、各社がそれぞれ希望する路線の工事を受注できるようもくろみ、すみ分ける形で受注を繰り返したとみられる。調整の上で複数社が入札に参加するケースもあれば、1社応札のケースもあり、落札額は1年契約で1社当たり数千万円から2億円台に上ることもあったという。【山田豊】

title: PayPay証券障害 日本株取引停止
body:
スマートフォン向けの証券会社PayPay証券でシステム障害が起きていて、日本株の取引ができなくなっています。【画像】「闇の市場」ダークウェブで売買される個人情報PayPay証券によりますと、午前10時15分以降、外部の接続先で障害が起き、日本株とETF＝上場投資信託の全ての銘柄の取引を停止しました。その後、午前11時30分ごろから1時間程度注文の受付を一時再開しましたが、障害の影響により現在は再び停止しているということです。14日の予約注文の受付も停止していて復旧のめどは立っていません。
アメリカ株や投資信託などの取引には影響は出ていないとしています。PayPay証券は不正アクセスではないとしていて、復旧に向けて対応を進めています。

title: JR東など7社 磁気乗車券を廃止へ
body: JR東日本や京成、京急、東武などの鉄道事業者7社は、磁気乗車券からQRコードを使用した乗車券へ置き換え、2027年春からQR乗車券サービスを開始する。参加する鉄道事業者は、京成電鉄、京浜急行電鉄、仙台空港鉄道、東京モノレール、東武鉄道、JR東日本(東日本旅客鉄道)、北総鉄道の7社。【この記事に関する別の画像を見る】券売機で購入できる「磁気乗車券」をQRコードを記した「QR乗車券」に置き換える取り組み。共通の仕組みやサーバーを導入することで、会社間をまたがるQR乗車券の発券・利用を可能とする。QR乗車券サービスは、鉄道7社の全路線、全駅で利用可能とするが、サービスを開始する事業者については、決まり次第各社より告知予定。磁気乗車券からQR乗車券への置き換えにあわせて、大型の乗車券に変更する。従来の磁気乗車券のサイズは30×57.5mmだが、QR乗車券は57.5×85mmとなる。また、改札の通過についても、入場時は磁気乗車券のように「投入」するのではなく、改札機のQRコードリーダーに「かざす」かたちとなる。出場時もかざしたうえで、回収箱に投入する。また、鉄道7社のQR乗車券を取り扱う自動改札機が設置されていない駅では、有人窓口を利用する。詳細については、決まり次第各社から告知する。また、相互直通運転などで関係する他の鉄道事業者とも、必要な調整を進めるとしている。長らく利用されてきた磁気乗車券だが、駅の自動改札機、自動券売機などの機器(出改札機器)、磁気乗車券用の機構の複雑さ・鉄道固有の専門性の高さから、中長期的な維持は難しいとされ、24年5月に各社が連携し、持続可能なシステムとしてQR乗車券へ移行すると発表していた。なお、24年の発表時には8社が協力するとしていたが、25年の京成電鉄と新京成電鉄の合併により、7社での磁気乗車券廃止、QR乗車券導入となる。

title: Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
summary: Pope Leo had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican said.
body:
Pope Leo arrived at Rome's Gemelli Hospital ahead of his surgery on Tuesday
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin.
The 71-year-old underwent a90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
"The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it added.
The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks". The Pope is expected to remain in hospital for about a week.
Earlier, large crowds waited for hours outside the hospital for the Pope.
They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car.
He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.
In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical".
A Vatican source told Agence France-Presse news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread.
It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.
He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.
Pope Leo XIV announced the news of his operation during his weekly Sunday prayers in Rome
Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.
The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.
He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.
The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.
Nuns were among those gathered outside the hospital where the Pope had surgery
Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world.
"Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.
He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.
Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.
Carla had come specially, wanting to be close.
"He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray."
"I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff.
"It turns out he's vulnerable too," she added.

title: Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
body:
Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000).

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
summary: Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany.
body:
Serhii K was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year
Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.
Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.
He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that  "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction,externaland prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects".
Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army,external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
summary: Sir Ken McCallum says operations to tackle terrorism and state threats are now roughly of an "equal scale".
body:
Watch: State threats and AI - Key takeaways from MI5 chief's speech
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.
Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.
At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".
He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones.
He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.
However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.
Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.
"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."
He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."
His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Asked after the speech aboutPrime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".
He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".
He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.
Sir Ken McCallum gave his annual address at MI5's headquarters in central London
Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK.
The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities.
Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites".
Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique".
He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK."
The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police.
Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".
The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response."
Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia.
On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual.
"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist."
Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes".
"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on."
Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are".
He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities".
In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely.
Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism.
He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent."
Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK".
He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

title: Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot
summary: The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa.
body:
The Houthi-run Yemen Petroleum Company assured residents of Sanaa that it had sufficient fuel supplies
Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.
The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran.
An Armaco administration building in Dhahran was also targeted, resulting in "limited fire", Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said in a statement.
No casualties were reported, the statement said.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.
The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.
A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".
The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".
After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices".
Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
summary: The CWU says more posties are leaving since a new delivery system was brought in, that it claims is not working in hundreds of offices.
body:
About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.
The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.
The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.
Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.
Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.
It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.
But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.
"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."
A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.
Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs
Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time
Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say
Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload.
We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day.
Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare".
"We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands.
Bryn Dymott says he is speaking out now because he wants people to know what's really happening
Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas.
"People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered."
Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening.
He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise."
So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices.
Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems.
The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others.
"Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU.
The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing.
Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas.
It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses."
The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period.
The BBC saw returned post that couldn't be delivered so ended up back on the frames in a Royal Mail office
Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans tocut 2,500 head office and other supporting rolesby the end of 2027.
The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out.
The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.
But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday.
"We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire.
"We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working."
An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us."
Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance."

title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?
summary: Graduates are increasingly using AI to misrepresent themselves in job applications, research suggests. But some say their peer group has no choice.
body:
Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?
Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?
We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications,graduates,externaland recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.
But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?
Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.
He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.
"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."
Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants
While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.
He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI whensome are using it themselves to screen candidates.
"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."
This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process".
According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.
However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.
On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.
EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees
Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.
EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.
Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.
"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."
Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.
It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills.
But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.
"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."
AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff'
AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts
Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI
One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.
While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.
"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"
According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.
And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving.
EDF does not currently use AI screening but Hollie Moody says they may have to in future.
She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.
"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
summary: The influential economics body has upgraded its UK growth forecast for this year, but risks remain.
body:
Countries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by  influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
What the IMF says matters – it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world.
Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel.
Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report.
The global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran.
The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise.
To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months.
Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI).
And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.
A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true.
There is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this.
The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.
Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both.
By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments.
"So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said.
Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany.
Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context.
"We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are."
While the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year.
While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest.
In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%.
"There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises,"  says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot.
He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year.

title: Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'
summary: The dating app which recently ditched its "women-first" chat rule has been bought by an investment firm.
body:
Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called "a bet on the future of humanity".
Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a "women-first" chat rule.
Bumble ditched the rule in August this year.
Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble's founder and current chief executive, said she would remain "actively involved" with the business she set up 12 years ago.
While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd's role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners.
Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to "renew and accelerate businesses...in a world transformed by AI".
They said: "Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfillment, human connection and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity."
This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, withsome experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity.
Bumble's share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reachedafter it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021.
Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023.
In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app.
Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had "exciting potential" in dating apps related to safety, and Bumble had been looking at research that found Gen Z and milliennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles.
This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles.
Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.
Itrecently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals.
"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.
Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.
Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.
Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.
Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.
According to a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.
Some single people are insteadturning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

title: Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
body:
Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000).

title: MI5 chief warns against overstating Russian interference in Brexit vote
summary: It comes after Andy Burnham said Moscow had tried to interfere in the 2016 referendum.
body:
MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum has said there was Russian interference in the the Brexit referendum, but warned against overstating its impact on the result.
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham provoked a backlash from some Brexit campaigners by saying it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow in the 2016 vote.
Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots.
However, he suggested Russian trolls would be "delighted" to be front page news again, "despite the comparative unimpressiveness" of their efforts.
He added: "There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall."
Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart branded Sir Ken's comments "an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister".
In an interview released on Monday, Burnham toldThe Rest is Politics podcast,externalthat upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."
He did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities during the interview, and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.
The PM denied claims from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch that he was implying the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference.
He said it was a "matter of record"that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, adding: "We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time".
A No 10 spokesperson also clarified that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.
The Conservatives accused Burnham of making an "embarrassing retreat" after "being caught out trying question the legitimacy of the referendum result".
It is inconceivable to think Russia did not try to interfere in Brexit vote, says PM
MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?
Answering questions after his annual speech at MI5's London headquarters earlier, Sir Ken said: "It is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.
"And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth."
He added that he agreed "strongly" with the PM that there was a hack and leak during the 2019 general election campaign.
However, he raised concerns about the impact of the debate on Russian interference.
"It is kind of up to us how far we allow our various adversaries to divide us," Sir Ken said.
"And I'm a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, that Russian trolls who didn't appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they'll be delighted because they are front page news again despite the comparative unimpressiveness of what they do at all points along the journey."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has accused Burnham of lying, saying there was "no Russian interference" in the referendum.
Meanwhile, former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary, the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".
He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told."
In 2020,a parliamentary reportdid not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian "troll" accounts on social media.

title: Argentina targets UK in legal claim over Falklands oil exploration
summary: The action filed with an international maritime tribunal is the latest development in an escalating row over the Falkland Islands.
body:
The Argentinian government has begun legal action seeking to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands in an escalating row with the UK.
Buenos Aires said in a statement the request lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea aimed to block activity authorised "illegally" by the UK.
The claim comes a fortnight after Argentinian President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies.
UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran criticised the "escalating campaign" from Argentina against companies operating in the Falklands, while announcing new protections for them.
The developments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the self-governing British territory, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentinian forces which had invaded the territory.
Earlier last month Milei also threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands.
Uma Kumaran accused the Argentinian government of "economic coercion" against the people of the Falkland Islands.
"We will do whatever it takes to support them," she told the House of Commons on Tuesday.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain.
The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom".
In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.
But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government.
While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary.
Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease".
The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly.
They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity.
They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion."
The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".
On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory".
Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.
UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year.

title: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
summary: The prime minister is calling for partners to step up support for Ukraine following Trump's criticism of Zelensky.
body:
Burnham met Zelensky at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.
Burnham is also expected to set out how his government will draw up further sanctions against Russia.
Speaking ahead of the meeting, Burnham said the UK was with Ukraine "for as long as it takes", adding: "Russian aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."
The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
This will be Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. His first was in late July, days after Burnham entered No 10, when the pair met troops and led a news conference at a naval base in Portsmouth.
Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.
"My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.
"It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do."
Among the measures being announced is the quicker delivery of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), with the UK having already committed to send more than 5,000 worth £1.6bn over the next four years.
The UK will also reaffirm its plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports.
The meeting between Zelensky and Burnham follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a "very difficult few days" for UK-US relations due to President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Zelensky criticised the US deal with Russia, calling it a "gift" to President Vladimir Putin. Trump, in response, called for new leadership in Ukraine and criticised Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries.
Meanwhile, Healey will ask partners at the IMF to step up support for Kyiv and ensure Russia heeds the US' call for a full energy ceasefire.
Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire - but hours later, Zelensky said Russian attacks on energy facilities had continued.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

title: Hundreds more prisoners being freed in second phase of early release scheme
summary: The second tranche of prisoners being released includes those serving up to two and a half years.
body:
Men were seen leaving HMP Durham
About 650 more offenders are leaving jails in England and Wales on Tuesday, in the second phase of the early release scheme - the government's plan to tackle the prison population crisis.
It includes offenders sentenced to up to two and a half years who are leaving jail after serving a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than half.
The second wave of releases comes as the government takes its plan to radically overhaul criminal courts back to Parliament - but also as probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to a strike over pay and workload.
Some 700 offenders left jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.
Tuesday's second stage begins the process of releasing batches of offenders on increasingly longer sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.
Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to be released, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to make rapists and the most serious child sex offenders exempt.
Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are also excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible. Those jailed for a range of offences, including members of child grooming gangs convicted of indecent assault are also ineligible.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said "the programme is clearly not working," stating she is "worried about dangerous people being let out on the street when they haven't served their sentence, haven't been rehabilitated".
Victims' groups have also raised concerns about the scheme.
Alice Russell-Harris from the charity Refuge - which supports survivors of domestic abuse - told the BBC that domestic abuse perpetrators are among those being released.
This "will put survivors at serious risk of harm," she said, adding that even though there may be conditions such as electronic tagging and restriction zones, "we know that license conditionsare frequently breached."
The early release scheme is "terrifying for survivors," said Veronica Oakeshott from the charity Women's Aid.
Reports of failures in the electronic tagging system have added to their concerns.  The scheme is "dangerous and should not go ahead," Oakeshott told the BBC.
A released prisoner is greeted by a friend as he leaves HMP Wandsworth prison in south London as part of the early release scheme
Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.
But the probation service union, Napo,said the releases put enormous strain on its members, who monitor offenders in the community.
Probation officers are "absolutely overwhelmed with work," Napo's general secretary Ian Lawrence told the BBC, saying those being released require "intensive supervision" and "the sheer weight of numbers causes pressure".
"None of our people go to work to see people injured, hurt, or for reoffending to happen," he said, but the numbers coming out means the probation service need more resources.
There are also concerns over delays in fitting electronic tags, which are used by probation officers to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order.
A report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) found that almost half of the tags used to track offenders are not fitted on time, withsome criminals waiting up to five months.
Official data which will show if there has been any improvement to electronic tagging will not be released for several months.
On Tuesday, the union's members will meet to discuss next week's vote, which could lead to strike action. Probation officers have been offered a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010.
The MoJ says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a £700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders.
Several people were released under the first tranche of the scheme are already back behind bars. Eight men were arrested by Greater Manchester Police (GMP)days after leaving prison under the government's early release scheme.
Five were arrested for breaches of criminal orders, including a domestic abuse prevention order, and others were held on suspicion of robbery, drug offences and domestic violence, GMP said.
While the second phase of prison releases gets under way, the government is bringing its criminal court reform plan back before MPs, after announcing a week ago that it had abandoned the most controversial element of it.
The revised plan drops proposals for a new form of Crown Court where a judge alone, sitting without a jury of ordinary people, would reach a verdict against suspects facing up to three years in prison.
However, jury trials will still be scrapped for the most complex and long fraud cases - and another 5,500 trials will be kept in the lower magistrates court by ending a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.
The government says it will expand the use of so-called "blitz" or "short trial" courts after pilots have shown that grouping similar cases together can speed up their progression through the courts - cutting backlogs.
One of the pilots at the Old Bailey led to the London backlog of 500 cases concerning assaults on emergency workers being cut in half over the summer.
A major review of criminal courts by former appeal judge Sir Brian Leveson recommended more virtual hearings for defendants to slash wasted time bringing them to and from cells. The government has now ordered pilots for defendants to appear direct from police cells.
On Monday, the government announced it had accepted more than 150 of his 180 recommendations to modernise the criminal courts.
It has rejected his advice to retain a restriction on volunteer magistrates that means they can only jail an offender for 12 months. Under the government's plan magistrates will have the power to jail for up to two years - the aim being to keep more cases out of Crown Court, to help clear backlogs.

title: UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year
summary: The prediction from the IMF comes as final preparations are being made for the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
body:
The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit the economy in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said.
The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.
Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".
Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.
Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.
Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.
But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies.
"As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said.
The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031.
Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".
The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economiesto cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.
While the IMF's forecasts are closely watched, the figures are only a prediction, a best estimate, of what will happen in the future. Forecasts often turn out to be incorrect due to world events.
Also, the chancellor's spending decisions at the Budget will be based on predictions from the UK's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, not the IMF.
The predictions in the IMF's latest World Economic Outlook suggest:
the UK is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany
UK growth is set to slow next year to 1.2% as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates hit household spending and business investment
UK inflation is expected to average 3.3% this year, and the IMF has increased its forecast for inflation next year to 2.8%.
the IMF said the global economy was "proving resilient" despite the ongoing war in the Middle East, helped by the investment surge in AI.
Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".
When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.
Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, told the BBC  the IMF's growth forecast was "better than it might have been", but noted that for 2027 it remained "more pessimistic".
"We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are," he added.
Sir Howard said the UK was "a bit of a sideshow" when it comes to the global economy and the IMF was more focused on how much the US is adding to its debt pile.
"That is what is putting pressure on interest rates all over the world and that is what is affecting us as well. Unless the US does something about its deficit, we can expect interest rates to be higher, which of course increases our debt interest costs," he said.
He added that the IMF was giving the UK credit in its forecast for tax rises which it might not end up actually putting through.
Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find£35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget.
On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes".
Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".
